## Pedagogical Training

::: {.publication-entry}
**[Kaufman Teaching Certificate Program (KTCP)](https://tll.mit.edu/programming/grad-student-programming/kaufman-teaching-certificate-program/)**

Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Fall 2024

<details>
<summary>Description</summary>

<p>I successfully completed a 10-workshop series focused on core teaching skills, including syllabus development, course design, lesson planning, student assessment and feedback, and fostering an effective and inclusive classroom environment. Two of the workshops were microteaching sessions, during which I delivered sample lessons on survey methodology in political science and received detailed feedback from peers and an experienced teaching mentor. As part of this program, I developed a course syllabus on public opinion and survey methodology, which I am happy to provide upon request.</p>
</details>
:::

## Teaching Assistant

::: {.publication-entry}
**17.279: Political Misinformation in the Age of Social Media**

Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Spring 2025 · Professor: Adam J. Berinsky

<details>
<summary>Description</summary>

<p>"Why are false and unsupported beliefs about politics and public policy so prevalent and hard to address? What role does social media play in the spread of misinformation? And what role should it play? This course explored the psychological factors that make people vulnerable to misperceptions and conspiracy theories and the reasons that attempts to counter false and extreme beliefs so often fail to reduce the prevalence of these phenomena. We paid especially close attention to the role of social media, and the internet more generally. We analyzed how the dynamics of misinformation and extreme beliefs are exploited by political elites and considered possible approaches that journalists, civic reformers, government officials, and technology platforms could employ to combat misperceptions. Students developed substantive expertise in how to measure, diagnose, and respond to false beliefs about politics and public policy; methodological expertise in reading and analyzing quantitative and experimental research in social science; and writing skills in preparing a final research paper analyzing the development of a specific misperception or conspiracy theory."</p>
</details>

<details>
<summary>Summary of Tasks</summary>

<p>I led and designed weekly, hour-long recitation sections that incorporated brief lectures, interactive activities, and guided discussions. These sessions provided students with opportunities to review course material, apply key concepts, engage with assigned readings, and clarify assignments and expectations. Recitation slides are available upon request. I also graded all written assessments and delivered a guest lecture on labeling AI-generated material online (slides available upon request).</p>
</details>

<details>
<summary>Student Evaluations</summary>

<p>Mean Student Rating: 6.7/7.0</p>

<p>"Student 9564 - Recitations were very well structured and helped synthesize the information presented earlier in the week. It especially helped for some of the longer readings, which were sometimes confusing. Dedicated time during the recitations to also discuss papers was extremely helpful, as it helped set expectations for different assignments. In summary, I truly enjoyed recitations and thought they heavily contributed to the bulk of my learning in classes. Gabby herself also demonstrated her passion within the subject, frequently bringing in outside examples, helping build context for the concepts being studied."</p>

<p>"Student 23736 - The interactive activities during recitation were enjoyable, and she explained lecture content in a comprehensible way."</p>
</details>
:::

::: {.publication-entry}
**17.263: Electoral Politics, Public Opinion, and Democracy**

Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Fall 2024 · Professor: Charles Stewart III

<details>
<summary>Description</summary>

<p>The purpose of this class was to examine the conduct of elections in the United States, with special attention to watching how the 2024 election evolved. "Considers the role of elections in American politics. Issues explored include empirical and theoretical models of electoral competition, the effect of elections on public policy, and proposals to improve elections. Special emphasis is given to mass voting behavior, political parties, the media, and campaign finance. Subject focuses on US elections, but provides some contrasts with other countries, especially the United Kingdom."</p>
</details>

<details>
<summary>Summary of Tasks</summary>

<p>I drafted reading quizzes for each lecture, graded all written and oral evaluations, held office hours to support students with course material and assessments, and taught two lectures on public opinion (slides available upon request).</p>
</details>

<details>
<summary>Student Evaluations</summary>

<p>Mean Student Evaluation: 6.8/7.0</p>

<p>"Student 10087 - Gabby is amazing; I really enjoyed the 2 lectures she taught on public opinion, which is one of the topics that I am personally most interested in. Gabby is (to my knowledge) in charge of grading most assignments. When I asked her to give me more individual feedback on a group project for which she had given the whole group the same feedback, she was willing to take the time to give me personal feedback, which I really appreciate"</p>

<p>"Student 42880 - Gabby was always very willing to help and gave very insightful feedback on papers"</p>
</details>
:::

## Instructor

::: {.publication-entry}
**Introduction to Causal Inference, [Pathways to Political Science Workshop](https://globaldiversitylab.mit.edu/summer-research-internship/)**

Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Summer 2025

<details>
<summary>Description</summary>

<p>I led a workshop introducing undergraduate and master's students in the Pathways to Political Science program at MIT to causal inference. The workshop provided an overview of counterfactual reasoning, the potential outcomes framework, experimental design, matching methods, regression analysis, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity designs, and difference-in-differences.</p>
</details>
:::

::: {.publication-entry}
**Introduction to Remote Resources, [Political Methodology Lab Workshop](https://pmlab.mit.edu/events/current-workshopsss/)**

Massachusetts Institute of Technology · Co-instructor with [Mason Reece](https://mreece13.github.io/)

Spring 2025

<details>
<summary>Description</summary>

<p>Alongside Mason Reece, I led a workshop for MIT Political Science PhD students as part of the Political Methodology Lab workshop series. The session introduced students to the Lab's high-performance computing system ([XVII](https://pmlab.mit.edu/computing/)) and [MIT Supercloud](https://supercloud.mit.edu/), an HPC-style shared computing cluster. We covered best practices for using these resources and provided Linux commands to help students begin working effectively on the Supercloud. Our slides can be accessed [here](pml_remote_slides.html).</p>
</details>
:::
